scenes.tts: A chick embryo makes about twenty thousand motor neurons for its legs. By about day ten, roughly twelve thousand are left. Nothing is wrong with this embryo. It has both legs, and it will hatch and walk. So where did the neurons go?

scenes.visual: A cluster of blue neuron dots beside a leg bud; a counter reads 20,000, then 40 percent of the dots turn red and vanish, leaving dashed ghosts, counter reads 12,000, and a question mark.

scenes.tts: Suppose you count only at the end, and the number is low. Maybe the cord divided too few times. Maybe it made enough cells, but sent too few to the place you counted. Maybe too few became the cell type you looked for. Or maybe the cells were made, and then lost. A final count looks the same in every case.
scenes.visual: Four histories appear one by one as chips, each with an arrow into the same short bar; the bar pulses each time; the last chip, made then lost, is red.
scenes.narration: Suppose you count only at the end, and the number is low. Maybe the cord divided too few times. Maybe it made enough cells, but sent too few to the place you counted. scenes.tts: To tell these apart, count at many times. Remove a wing bud from one side of chick embryos. Then take embryos at closely spaced stages. In each one, compare the operated side with the intact side. Count the healthy motor neurons, and count the dying cells, which have dark, condensed nuclei. If the neurons were never made, the operated side is low from the first count, with no burst of dying cells. If they were made and then lost, the two sides start equal. Then dying cells appear, and the operated side falls behind.
scenes.visual: Two empty plots gain time ticks; legend chips for operated side, intact side and dying cells. Left plot: operated curve low from the start, no red dots. Right plot: curves start together, red dots burst, operated curve falls away. A chip for the wing bud removal comes first.
scenes.narration: To tell these apart, count at many times. Remove a wing bud from one side of chick embryos. Then take embryos at closely spaced stages. scenes.tts: In 1975, Hamburger counted the death itself, in normal embryos with all their limbs. The motor neurons that serve the leg peaked at just over twenty thousand, between days five and a half and six and a half. They settled near twelve thousand after day nine and a half. That is a loss of about forty percent, in his uncorrected counts. Most of it came between days six and a half and nine and a half.

scenes.visual: One real count curve is drawn: peak band, then the fall to a plateau, a red bracket for the 40 percent loss, a red band over the days when most was lost.

scenes.tts: Hollyday and Hamburger tested the logic from the other direction. They grafted an extra leg onto chick embryos. At day six, before the normal loss, the grafted side had no more motor neurons than the control. Later, in embryos whose grafts moved vigorously, it had more. About eleven to twenty-eight percent more.

scenes.visual: A cord with a leg and a dashed extra leg; a plot where the grafted yellow curve sits on the control at day six, then ends higher than the control, with a label for the gap.

scenes.tts: More target did not mean more births. It meant fewer deaths. These results suggested that the target supplies something limited that the neurons need to survive. So a final count hides its own history. Count across time, and you can tell neurons never made from neurons made and lost.
scenes.visual: Two stacked bars with the same made height; in the extra-leg bar the red lost part shrinks. Question-mark covers hide the red parts, then the bars give way to the two time plots, never made and made then lost.
